episodes.181389: Two rounds of thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours of July 29, 2023. The first round during the afternoon was the most severe, taking advantage of plentiful amounts of daytime instability. Damaging winds were common with these storms with the most notable damage occurring in Green Hill where a microburst uprooted and damaged multiple trees and power poles. The second round of thunderstorms during the evening arrived as a weakening squall line, producing wind speeds of 40 to 55 mph.
episodes.181482: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening, one of which produced wind damage.
episodes.181491: A cold front moved through northeast Montana producing strong to severe thunderstorms.
episodes.181492: Afternoon surface heating combined with an embedded disturbance, which generated multiple strong to severe thunderstorms which lasted into the nighttime hours.
episodes.181579: Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across Virginia ahead of a surface trough and cold front across the Ohio Valley and southern Appalachian region. These storms produced locally damaging winds across the northern and northwest Piedmont of central North Carolina in the evening hours. Storms then weakened with southeastern extent over the central and eastern Piedmont to Coastal Plain by late evening.
episodes.181580: A southward moving cold front and an upper-level disturbance over Tennessee and Kentucky led to development of isolated thunderstorms over the southern Piedmont of central North Carolina during the late-afternoon and evening. One storm became severe over Anson county, producing wind damage in Polkton and Peachland.
episodes.181671: Scattered mostly dry thunderstorms developed on the afternoon on the 28th with subsequent lightning leading to a fire that damaged a local hay crop.
episodes.181920: A bowing line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved rapidly southeast from southern Illinois across far western Kentucky. This line was associated with numerous pockets of wind damage. The line of storms moved through a strongly unstable air mass during the heat of the day, when mixed-layer capes were as high as 3000 j/kg. A similar airmass extended east into western Kentucky, which helped the storms maintain organization as they moved east-southeastward through the lower Ohio Valley.
episodes.181931: A strong cold front intersected a very hot, humid, and unstable airmass across the Mid-Atlantic shortly after peak heating. Aided by dynamics and moderately strong shear from an approaching upper-level trough, the front spawned bands of thunderstorms that produced considerable wind damage particularly in the I-95 corridor. Some areas saw the worst thunderstorm-driven wind speeds and damage since the derecho in June 2012, though the area affected by the highest magnitude of winds was not nearly as large.
episodes.181946: A strong cold front intersected a very hot, humid, and unstable airmass across the Mid-Atlantic shortly after peak heating. Aided by dynamics and moderately strong shear from an approaching upper-level trough, the front spawned bands of thunderstorms that produced up to storm-force winds over area waterways.
episodes.182045: After a period of quiet weather, several days of strong to severe thunderstorms occurred during the latter part of July. Chinook was struck the hardest with up to baseball size hail resulting in significant vehicle and structural damage. Harlem and Fort Belknap also received severe hail. Additional severe storms impacted the east side of Great Falls, Belt, and Lewistown with large hail being reported in all three locations.

episodes.182098: A mean westerly steering flow pushed a progressive Gulf sea breeze inland and pinned the Atlantic sea breeze between I-95 and the Atlantic coast in the afternoon where explosive convection developed over a very moist and unstable airmass. Additional strong to severe storms developed across SE GA near a meandering surface front, but coverage was limited given drier mean layer moisture.

episodes.182279: An upper level ridge extended from the Desert Southwest and south Texas northward to Nebraska and Wyoming. During the early to mid-morning hours, the temperature was in the mid to upper 60s and the dewpoint was also in the mid to upper 60s across south central Nebraska. In the early evening hours, the temperature was in the 80s and the dewpoint was in the mid 60s to lower 70s. There was subtle low to mid-level warm air advection/isentropic ascent across portions of eastern Nebraska during the morning hours. During the early evening hours, the effective wind shear was generally 40 to 50 knots and the most unstable CAPE was 3,000 to 5,000 J/kg. Mid-level lapse rates were generally between 7 to 8 degrees C/km. ||Storms developed and moved across south central Nebraska during the morning hours. One storm moved into Clay County and produced one inch hail just after 8 AM CDT. This storm weakened and moved out of the area later in the morning. Storms redeveloped across south central Nebraska during the afternoon hours. One storm strengthened and moved into Thayer County and produced one inch hail just after 7 PM CDT. This storm then moved southward into Kansas.
episodes.182735: A long-lived supercell thunderstorm tracked from southwestern North Dakota across portions of northwestern and west central South Dakota during the evening hours. The storm produced large hail and wind gusts around 70 mph along its path.
episodes.182736: A supercell thunderstorm developed over the central Black Hills, producing very large hail larger than baseballs from Pactola Reservoir to Sheridan Lake and eastward to the Rockerville area.
episodes.182741: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over northeastern Campbell County, producing large hail north of Weston.
episodes.182744: A long-lived supercell thunderstorm developed along the Montana border in northern Campbell County and tracked southeast through far northeastern Wyoming. The storm produced large hail and very strong wind gusts to 80 mph, causing considerable damage in some areas.
episodes.182757: Thunderstorms developed over western North Dakota in an environment with strong deep layer shear and elevated instability. Some of these storms became severe, producing large hail and strong wind gusts. The largest hail reported was the size of a golf ball, which occurred near Oakdale and near Twin Buttes, both in Dunn County. The strongest wind gust reported was 79 mph at the Grassy Butte NDAWN station in McKenzie County.
episodes.182764: Thunderstorms formed during the early morning hours as an upper level short-wave moved into an environment of enhanced instability and strong deep layer shear. Some of these storms became severe over southwest and south central North Dakota, producing large hail. The largest hail reported was the size of a golf ball, and fell in Grant County south of Brisbane.
episodes.182813: A shortwave disturbance and potent cold front brought multiple rounds of thunderstorms to Massachusetts in the afternoon and evening including a tornado in the Foxboro area. Flash flooding was also an issue with many cars becoming stuck in water and many closed roads.
episodes.182814: A shortwave disturbance and potent cold front brought multiple rounds of thunderstorms to Rhode Island in the afternoon and evening.

episodes.183132: A persistent northwest flow aloft coupled with a moist, unstable environment allowed for multiple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms to develop each afternoon. The storms moved generally from north to south across the area, with much of the wind damage occurring in the afternoon/evening hours.
episodes.183287: Thunderstorms developed along a warm front during the morning, bringing severe weather to central and north central South Dakota. The storms produced quarter size to golfball size hail, with the latter falling in Akaska.
episodes.183320: Storms developed in the afternoon as an upper-level short-wave moved across the area. Unorganized storms developed and produced a few hail reports with the largest reported hailstone being 2-inches near Creston in Madison County. There was also a single wind report of 65-mph near Thurston.
episodes.183396: Storms developed in the afternoon as an upper-level short-wave moved across the area. Unorganized storms developed and produced 1.25-inch hail in western Pottawattamie County.
episodes.183538: Storms that developed along the advancing cold front on the evening of the 29th produced damaging wind gusts mainly along and south of Highway 60 from Monett to West Plains. Rainfall accumulations averaged between one-half inch and one and a half inches.
episodes.183600: An unusually strong upper level disturbance dropped southward from the northern Plains into western Missouri during the evening of the 30th and continued southward through the early morning of the 31st. Widespread wind gusts measured over 70 mph affected locations from Fort Scott to Lamar to South Springfield to Branson, resulting in widespread power outages from downed trees and powerlines. Some locations were without power for several days as a result of these storms.
episodes.183602: An upper level area of low pressure and and associated cold front dropped into the the Mid-Atlantic region. Storms erupted by midday, aided in part by large-scale forcing, but also driven by diurnal heating and unstable air. A few organized clusters of storms produced wind damage across the area.
episodes.183788: Severe thunderstorms produced large hail in Logan and Morgan counties.  Hail up to tennis ball size was observed in Logan County, with hail up to quarter size in Morgan County.
episodes.183833: Clusters of strong thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon hours ahead of a cold front across central Georgia. These thunderstorms then tracked to the east through the evening into southeast Georgia and produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183878: Scattered thunderstorms developed and moved west across portions of southeast Arizona during the late afternoon and evening. Thunderstorm winds caused damage in southeast Tucson.
episodes.183897: A weak mid-level wave set off discrete hail producing thunderstorms across southeast South Dakota during the late morning and early afternoon.
episodes.183898: A weak mid-level wave set off discrete hail producing thunderstorms across northeast Nebraska during the afternoon.
episodes.183953: Severe weather made it into places near the Missouri border during the evening of the 29th. Trees were flattened at Ash Flat (Sharp County), Black Rock (Lawrence County), and Gamaliel (Baxter County). Early on the 31st, power outages were widespread in Boone and Marion Counties (due to lightning and wind). A shed was destroyed at Damascus (Van Buren County).
episodes.184002: A line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms moved into western North Carolina from east Tennessee during the late afternoon and evening. Isolated embedded cells produced locally damaging wind gusts.

episodes.184253: Deep monsoon moisture allowed for the development of a strong thunderstorm north of Supai. This caused a flash flood in Havasu Creek.

episodes.184388: Surface flow from the east advected amply amounts of low level moisture which created another event where heavy rains, hail, and gusty winds were observed. Weak perturbations in the upper flow sparked thunderstorms across the region.
episodes.184420: Northwest flow in the mid- and upper-levels of the atmosphere placed central Kentucky and southern Indiana on the edge of a ring of fire type pattern for several days at the end of July 2023. While most of the waves of convection remained to the north of the area thanks to building ridging aloft July 27th into the 28th, thunderstorms on July 27th clipped the Kentucky Bluegrass region. The primary impact from these storms were heavy amounts of rainfall, with over 5 inches of rain being reported at a CoCoRaHS station in Nicholas County. This resulted in scattered instances of flash flooding across Nicholas, Harrison, and Bourbon County, Kentucky late in the evening on July 27th into the early morning hours on July 28th. Sadly, one fatality resulted from a home being swept away in Nicholas County.||Otherwise, conditions were mainly quiet across the region until the early morning hours of July 29th, when a mid-level trough began to dig southwestward into the Ohio Valley, allowing a surface frontal boundary to sink closer to the region, placing central Kentucky and southern Indiana into a more convectively active domain. A bowing mesoscale convective system moved from the mid-Mississippi valley eastward into Kentucky and extreme southern Indiana during the late evening hours on July 29th. While this system was generally dissipating as it moved through the area, it still retained enough strength to cause sporadic wind damage across central Kentucky and southern Indiana.
